## Simple explanation

Wasserstein distance measures how much work it takes to reshape one
probability distribution into another by moving probability mass.

## Technical explanation

For distributions $P$ and $Q$ on a metric space with ground cost $d$, the
$p$-Wasserstein distance is
$W_p(P,Q)=\left(\inf_{\gamma\in\Pi(P,Q)}\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\gamma}[d(x,y)^p]\right)^{1/p}$.
Here, $\Pi(P,Q)$ is the set of joint distributions whose marginals are $P$
and $Q$. Unlike divergences that may be infinite for disjoint supports,
Wasserstein distance can reflect how far apart the supports are, given the
chosen geometry and moment conditions.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

It is used in optimal transport, generative modeling, and comparing
distributions. The ground metric and computational approximation shape the
result; practical implementations may use regularization or specialized
estimators.

## How it works

Consider all possible couplings that move mass from samples of $P$ to samples
of $Q$. Measure transport cost under each coupling and select the minimum.
Exact optimization can be expensive, especially for large empirical
distributions.

## Practical example

Compare generated and real one-dimensional distributions by computing a
transport cost over their samples. A low value only indicates similarity under
the selected metric and sampling procedure; it is not a complete evaluation of
generative quality.

## Common misconceptions

- Wasserstein distance is not a universal measure of distribution quality; it
  depends on the ground metric and data representation.
- The optimal transport plan is not necessarily a one-to-one pairing of
  samples.
